issues.legal_issue: Property acquired with waqf funds for a waqf remains waqf property even when acquired in the name of a beneficiary.
material_facts: A valid Shia family waqf had been created, and the disputed land and bungalow related to one division of the waqf.
The land was leased in the name of a beneficiary, who was the mutawalli’s wife, but the courts found that the lease and construction were paid for from waqf funds under the mutawalli’s direction.
The evidence did not establish that the beneficiary paid for the property from her personal funds.
issues.conclusion: The property belonged to the waqf estate; the beneficiary held its apparent title as a benamidar.
issues.legal_principle: Under Shia law, a waqf is irrevocable after possession is given, and its corpus is tied up for the waqf’s objects while its usufruct is applied to those objects. A mutawalli is a manager, not the owner of waqf property. Property acquired by a mutawalli from waqf proceeds becomes part of the waqf and does not cease to be waqf property merely because title is taken in a beneficiary’s name. The Court relied on Tyabji’s Muslim Law and Ameer Ali’s Mohammedan Law, explained Moattar Raza v. Joint Director of Consolidation, and rejected the contrary statement in Mohammad Qamar Shah Khan v. Mohammad Salamat Ali Khan.

rule.if: waqf_property_dispute and waqf_funds_paid_for_acquisition and manager_directed_use_of_funds and title_taken_in_beneficiary_name

predicates.waqf_property_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether property acquired for or connected with a waqf belongs to the waqf estate.
predicates.waqf_funds_paid_for_acquisition: Money from the waqf estate paid for the property’s acquisition or construction.
predicates.manager_directed_use_of_funds: The person managing the waqf directed or controlled the use of its funds for the acquisition or construction.
predicates.title_taken_in_beneficiary_name: Title to the acquired property was placed in the name of a waqf beneficiary.

issues.definition: When a property dispute concerns an acquisition paid for with waqf funds under the waqf manager’s direction and title is placed in a beneficiary’s name, the property remains waqf property.

issues.legal_issue: A waqf manager cannot use waqf income to acquire immovable property for one beneficiary in disregard of the other beneficiaries and thereby make it that beneficiary’s private property.
material_facts: The waqf deed gave the mutawalli power to fix stipends for beneficiaries, but the waqf had numerous beneficiaries.
The disputed bungalow was acquired and built with waqf funds for the benefit of the mutawalli’s wife.
The deed treated property purchased from the estate’s funds as belonging to the waqf, and the evidence did not show a valid personal payment to the wife.
issues.conclusion: The mutawalli had no authority to use waqf funds to acquire the property for his wife alone, and the acquisition remained a waqf asset.
issues.legal_principle: A mutawalli, though not a trustee in the technical sense, is bound by fiduciary obligations and cannot use the position to advance his own interests or unduly favour one beneficiary over others. The power to fix stipends must be exercised reasonably and consistently with the principles of Mohammedan law; it does not authorize an disproportionate expenditure to acquire immovable property for one beneficiary. The Court relied on the waqf deed’s provisions governing stipends and property bought from estate funds, and on the general duties of a trustee and a mutawalli described in Tyabji’s Muslim Law and Ameer Ali’s Mohammedan Law.

rule.if: waqf_administration_dispute and manager_used_waqf_income_for_immovable_property and acquisition_favoured_one_beneficiary and other_beneficiaries_were_disregarded

predicates.waqf_administration_dispute: The proceeding concerns how a waqf manager used or administered waqf funds.
predicates.manager_used_waqf_income_for_immovable_p: The waqf manager used income or funds of the waqf to acquire or construct immovable property.
predicates.acquisition_favoured_one_beneficiary: The acquisition was made for the individual benefit of one beneficiary rather than for the waqf’s purposes generally.
predicates.other_beneficiaries_were_disregarded: The manager’s use of funds disregarded the interests of the waqf’s other beneficiaries.

issues.definition: If a waqf manager uses waqf income to acquire immovable property for one beneficiary while disregarding the others, the manager cannot make that acquisition private property.

issues.legal_issue: In a waqf-funded acquisition placed in a beneficiary’s name, the usual rules governing proof of a benami transaction do not apply in full, and a presumption arises that the property belongs to the waqf.
material_facts: The courts found that the waqf estate funded the lease and construction of the disputed property.
The property was acquired in the name of a beneficiary, while the waqf manager controlled the funds used for the acquisition.
The beneficiary did not establish that the property was acquired with her personal funds, and the principal test of the source of the purchase money supported the waqf’s claim.
issues.conclusion: The findings that the beneficiary was a benamidar for the waqf were sustainable; once waqf funding was established, it was for the beneficiary to establish that the property was personal rather than waqf property.
issues.legal_principle: Ordinarily, the person asserting that a transaction is benami bears a strict burden of proof, and the source of the purchase money is the most important test. The Court relied on Gopeekrist Gosain v. Gangaparsaud Gosain, Bilas Kunwar v. Desraj Ranjit Singh, Kerwick v. Kerwick, Sura Lakshmiah Chetty v. Kothandarama Pillai, Gangadara Ayyar v. Subramania Sastrigal, Kalwa Devadattam v. Union of India, Union of India v. Moksh Builders, Jaydayal Poddar v. Bibi Hazra and Krishnanand v. State of Madhya Pradesh. It held that the benami rules, including the usual burden, cannot be applied in full where the property was acquired with waqf funds; proof of that funding raises a presumption that the property is waqf property, leaving the ostensible owner to establish personal ownership.

rule.if: benami_property_dispute and waqf_funds_paid_for_acquisition and manager_controlled_acquisition_funds and property_titled_to_beneficiary

predicates.benami_property_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether the person named as purchaser or titleholder is the real owner of property.
predicates.waqf_funds_paid_for_acquisition: Money from a waqf estate paid for the property’s acquisition or construction.
predicates.manager_controlled_acquisition_funds: The waqf manager controlled or directed the use of the funds paid for the acquisition.
predicates.property_titled_to_beneficiary: Title to the property was placed in the name of a waqf beneficiary.

issues.definition: In a benami property dispute, where a waqf manager controlled funds from the waqf used to acquire property titled to a beneficiary, the property is presumed to belong to the waqf unless the beneficiary proves personal ownership.

issues.legal_issue: A party cannot obtain relief on a materially new case raised on appeal when the case was not advanced at trial and the opposing party had no opportunity to meet it.
material_facts: At trial, the beneficiary claimed that she acquired the property with her personal funds; the opposing party contended that waqf funds paid for it.

In the High Court, the beneficiary advanced a different case based on her husband’s personal funds, and in the Supreme Court she argued that waqf income used for the acquisition had become her personal money.
The parties had adduced evidence and tried the case on the source of the acquisition funds, not on the new theory advanced in the Supreme Court.
issues.conclusion: The beneficiary could not rely on the new theory in the Supreme Court, and it did not provide a basis for granting her claim.
issues.legal_principle: Pleadings are construed in light of the stand taken at trial and the issues on which the parties adduced evidence and argued. Relief cannot ordinarily be granted on a case that had no foundation in the pleadings and that the opposing party was not called on to meet. The Court distinguished Srinivas Ram Kumar v. Mahabir Prasad, Nagubai Ammal v. B. Shama Rao and Kunju Kesavan v. M. M. Philip, where the opposing party had admitted, raised, or tried the alternative matter and was not prejudiced by its consideration.

rule.if: civil_appeal and appellant_raises_new_material_case and case_not_tried_on_that_basis and opposing_party_had_no_opportunity_to_meet_it

predicates.civil_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal in a civil dispute.
predicates.appellant_raises_new_material_case: The appellant advances on appeal a materially different factual or legal basis for the requested relief.
predicates.case_not_tried_on_that_basis: The parties did not adduce evidence or conduct the trial on the basis of that new case.
predicates.opposing_party_had_no_opportunity_to_mee: The opposing party was not called on during the trial to answer the new case.

issues.definition: If a civil appellant advances a material case that was not tried and the other party had no opportunity to meet it, that new case cannot support relief.

issues.legal_issue: A waqf benefit for descendants is distributed per capita equally among male and female beneficiaries, including the children of daughters, unless the waqf instrument shows a different intention.
material_facts: The waqf was created primarily for the benefit of the settler’s family and descendants.
The deed provided for distribution among family beneficiaries, and the dispute concerned whether the mutawalli could use the available income disproportionately for one beneficiary.
The Court considered the deed’s provisions alongside the general rule for distributing a waqf benefit to descendants.
issues.conclusion: In the absence of a different intention in the waqf instrument, descendants take the benefit per capita, males and females equally, and the children of daughters are included.
issues.legal_principle: Tyabji’s Muslim Law, section 545(4), states that a waqf benefit for a person’s sons, children and further descendants is taken per capita, with males and females taking equally and the children of daughters included, unless a different intention appears. The Court explained Ahmed G. H. Ariff v. Commissioner of Wealth Tax, Calcutta, and held it inapplicable because it concerned the treatment of a beneficiary’s income interest as an asset for wealth-tax purposes.

predicates.waqf_income_distribution_dispute: The proceeding concerns how distributable income or benefits of a waqf are allocated among beneficiaries.
predicates.waqf_benefits_descendants: The waqf provides a benefit for descendants of the settler or another identified person.
predicates.instrument_shows_no_different_intention: The waqf instrument does not show an intention to distribute the benefit differently.

issues.definition: When a waqf benefits descendants and its instrument shows no different intention, the descendants share the benefit per capita equally.

issues.legal_issue: Concurrent factual findings supported by the evidence should not be disturbed on special-leave appeal when no infirmity in those findings is established.
material_facts: The trial court and High Court both found that the disputed property was funded by the waqf estate and that the beneficiary did not establish personal ownership.
The documentary and oral evidence supported those findings, particularly the evidence tracing the acquisition and construction expenses to waqf funds.
The appellant did not successfully challenge the primary factual findings and relied on a new theory that the Court rejected.
issues.conclusion: The Court found no basis to interfere with the concurrent findings and dismissed the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: In reviewing concurrent factual findings on special leave, the Court does not ordinarily reappraise findings that are supported by the evidence and disclose no infirmity. The Court referred to Meenakshi Mills v. Commissioner of Income-tax and the principles concerning findings based on evidence discussed in Gangadara Ayyar v. Subramania Sastrigal; it did not need to decide which side of the general line of review the case occupied because the primary findings were clearly supported.

rule.if: special_leave_civil_appeal and lower_courts_made_concurrent_factual_findings and findings_supported_by_evidence and no_material_infirmity_shown

predicates.special_leave_civil_appeal: The proceeding is a civil appeal brought by special leave.
predicates.lower_courts_made_concurrent_factual_fin: The trial court and the appellate court below reached the same factual findings.
predicates.findings_supported_by_evidence: The findings are supported by evidence in the record.
predicates.no_material_infirmity_shown: The appellant has not established a material flaw in the concurrent findings.

issues.definition: In a civil appeal by special leave, concurrent findings supported by the record are left undisturbed when no material infirmity is shown.
